Chapter 2: Focusing on Systems Instead of Goals
Let's dive into something that trips up a lot of people—putting all your energy into ambitious goals and hoping that just having a target will get you where you want to go.
Sure, goals help point you in the right direction, but here's the catch: it's actually your systems—those everyday routines and little habits—that really drive your progress.
Think about it like this. Imagine a gardener who dreams of a lush, beautiful garden. The harvest is the goal, right? But what actually makes those flowers and veggies grow? It's the system—things like regular watering, pulling weeds, and just taking care of the soil day in and day out.
Goals can light a fire under you and give you that push to get started, but they're often short-lived. After you hit a goal, motivation can just fizzle out, and before you know it, those old habits sneak back in.
But systems—they keep you moving forward, no matter what. They're about creating a structure for steady, ongoing improvement, not just chasing after one big result.
So why do systems work better than just focusing on goals? Well, there are a few good reasons:
First, Sustained Progress. When you lean into systems, you're more likely to keep taking action, even after you hit a milestone. It's like building momentum that carries you further each day.
Second, Reduced Pressure. When your attention is on the process, not the outcome, it takes so much pressure off. You're not stressing over instant results, which makes it easier to bounce back from setbacks.
And third, Identity Change. Systems help you become the kind of person you want to be, not just someone chasing after a finish line.
Let me give you an example. Let's say you want to write a novel. You might set a goal to finish a manuscript in six months. Sounds good, right? But if you focus instead on writing just one page every day, suddenly, it's manageable. Over time, you're not just finishing a book—you’re actually becoming a writer, every single day you show up to write.
This idea works for breaking bad habits, too. Instead of obsessing over quitting smoking, you shift your attention to building a system that makes smoking less tempting, and healthier choices easier to stick with.
One simple, powerful question to ask yourself is: What kind of person would achieve this outcome? Then, focus on showing up as that person in small, consistent ways. Instead of thinking, "I want to run a marathon," you start acting like someone who never misses a workout.
When you make this shift—from chasing far-off goals to building everyday systems—progress feels almost effortless. The journey becomes less about the results, and more about enjoying the process of growing, one step at a time.
